QuestionStmt.S: The lines $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$ and $\vec{r} = \vec{c} + \lambda (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$ will intersect if

Solution.S:
The line $\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$ passes through $\vec{a}$ and is parallel to $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}$.

The line $\vec{r} = \vec{c} + \lambda (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$ passes through $\vec{c}$ and is parallel to $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$.

For intersection, the vectors $\vec{a} - \vec{c}$, $\vec{b} \times \vec{c}$, and $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ must be coplanar.

$$(\vec{a} - \vec{c}) \cdot [(\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) \times (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})] = 0$$

Using vector identity, this simplifies to:

$$(\vec{a} - \vec{c}) \cdot \vec{b} = 0 \Rightarrow \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}$$

Thus, the lines intersect if $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}$.

Final Answer: $$\boxed{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}}$$

Hence, the correct option is B.
